script.opening: "Doctor, I've had this awful pain in the lower right side of my tummy since I woke up. I've never had anything like this before. I don't know what to do."

facts.text: Constant cramping, gradually worsening over 8 hours. 6/10 at rest, 8/10 if she moves. No radiation. Sharp twinge if she coughs.
Nausea, no vomiting. Light brown spotting on the toilet paper this afternoon — first time she's noticed. No urinary symptoms, no bowel symptoms.
Periods usually regular every 28 days; last period was approximately 6 weeks ago. She thinks she might be late, hasn't tested.
Came off the COCP 4 months ago because she and her husband had started trying for a baby.
Chlamydia treated aged 19. One episode of laparoscopic surgery for an ovarian cyst at 23.
Reports lightheadedness if she stands up too quickly. Some left shoulder-tip ache she dismissed as sleeping awkwardly.

ice.ideas: Thinks it might be appendicitis like her cousin had.
ice.concerns: Frightened — she's been trying to get pregnant and is worried she might lose a baby she didn't know she had.
ice.expectations: Wants the GP to tell her whether to go to A&E or wait it out.

cues: Mentions "we've been trying" — invitation to discuss pregnancy.
Goes quiet when asked about shoulder pain.
Says "I really thought we'd be lucky this month".

checkpoints.text: Recognises ectopic pregnancy as the leading differential and asks about LMP, contraception, and intercourse
Elicits red flags: shoulder-tip pain, lightheadedness, bleeding
Arranges same-day Early Pregnancy Unit (EPAU) or A&E review — does NOT plan a routine GP review
Advises urine pregnancy test before leaving home, but does not delay transfer waiting for the result
Acknowledges the emotional weight ("you've been trying for a baby")
Uses plain language about ectopic pregnancy — explains why this is urgent without frightening
Safety-nets clearly: 999 if collapse / severe sudden worsening / heavy bleeding
Confirms transport and whether husband / family are available

worked.txt: "Layla, I want to hear the story in your own words first — what's the pain been doing since you noticed it this morning?"
"You mentioned your period is late — and you've been trying. That makes me want to think carefully about pregnancy as part of this picture."
"One of the things we always have to rule out with this kind of pain is a pregnancy that's settled outside the womb — that's called an ectopic — and that's why I want you seen today, not tomorrow."
"I can hear how much this matters. Whatever this turns out to be, you're doing the right thing by ringing now."
"If you feel suddenly faint, the pain gets dramatically worse, or you start bleeding heavily — that's a 999 call, not a wait."

f.learning: Any woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain has an ectopic until proven otherwise — LMP, contraception, sexual activity. Shoulder-tip pain and orthostatic symptoms shift the probability sharply. EPAU is the destination, not a routine GP review. The emotional layer here — "we've been trying" — is the marking difference between Pass and Clear pass.

knowledge.summary: Any woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain is an ectopic until proven otherwise. The destination is a same-day Early Pregnancy Assessment Unit, not a routine GP review.

points.t: Always establish LMP, contraception and possibility of pregnancy. A positive/uncertain pregnancy test with pain (or bleeding at ≥6 weeks, uncertain gestation or with ectopic risk factors) mandates same-day EPAU assessment; 999/A&E if haemodynamically unstable.

points.h: Red flags that raise ectopic risk
points.t: Shoulder-tip pain, dizziness/syncope, rectal pressure, haemodynamic compromise, lateralised pain. Risk factors: previous ectopic, PID/chlamydia, tubal surgery, IUD, assisted conception.

points.h: Don’t let the test delay transfer
points.t: Advise a urine βhCG but do not wait for it before arranging review if clinical suspicion is high; in EPAU, serial serum βhCG + transvaginal USS guide management.
999 for collapse, severe sudden worsening, or heavy bleeding. Be clear it’s an emergency pathway, not “see how it goes”.
Appendicitis, ovarian torsion, ruptured/haemorrhagic cyst, PID, UTI — but ectopic is the can’t-miss diagnosis driving the urgency.
Naming and holding the emotional weight (“you’ve been trying for a baby”) while acting decisively is what separates Pass from Clear pass.

model.text: Hello Layla, I’m the duty GP. I can hear you’re uncomfortable — I want the story in your own words first. What’s the pain been doing since you noticed it this morning?
model.why: Open question, builds rapport with a worried caller

model.text: I woke up with this awful pain low down on the right. It’s been getting worse all day. I’ve never had anything like it.
Can you describe it — constant or in waves, and does anything make it worse?
Constant, cramping. About a six, but eight if I move. Sharp twinge if I cough.
Any nausea or vomiting, and any change to your waterworks or bowels?
A bit sick, not actually sick. Nothing with bladder or bowels. I did notice some light brown spotting this afternoon, though.
Thank you, that’s important. Can I ask about your periods — when was your last one?
model.why: Moves to pregnancy risk early in a woman of reproductive age

model.text: That’s the thing — about six weeks ago. I’m usually bang on 28 days. I haven’t tested.
And are you using any contraception at the moment?
No — we came off the pill four months ago, we’ve been trying for a baby.
Have you felt lightheaded or dizzy at all, or had any pain at the tip of your shoulder?
model.why: Screens specifically for ectopic red flags

model.text: Now you say it — I felt faint standing up earlier. And there’s a dull ache in my left shoulder. I thought I’d slept on it.
Have you ever had an ectopic pregnancy, a pelvic infection, or surgery on your tubes or ovaries?
I had chlamydia years ago, and an operation for an ovarian cyst at 23.
Before I tell you what I’m thinking — what’s gone through your own mind about what this might be?
I’m terrified I’m losing a baby. Or that something’s really wrong.
I can hear how frightening this is, and I’m going to be honest and careful with you because that’s the safest thing.

The combination of a late period, this pain, the spotting, feeling faint and the shoulder ache means I have to take seriously the possibility of a pregnancy that has settled outside the womb — an ectopic. That needs checking today, not tomorrow.
model.why: Reaches the working diagnosis; does not falsely reassure

model.text: Oh god. So it could be an ectopic?
It’s on my list and I can’t rule it out over the phone — that’s exactly why I want you seen properly. Whatever this turns out to be, ringing now was absolutely the right thing to do.
model.why: Honest about uncertainty; affirms the patient’s action

model.text: Here’s my plan. I’m going to arrange for you to be seen today at the Early Pregnancy Unit — they’ll do a scan and a blood test. If there’s any delay getting there, or you feel worse, it’s A&E instead. Does that sound manageable?
model.why: Same-day EPAU/A&E referral with a clear route

model.text: Yes. My husband’s at work but I’ll call him.
Good. Do a home pregnancy test if you have one handy, but please don’t wait for it before you set off — the assessment matters more than the test.
model.why: Does not delay definitive assessment for a home test

model.text: Okay. Should I take any painkillers?
Paracetamol is fine, but nothing that would mask things, and don’t eat or drink much in case they need to act quickly. I’ll phone the unit now so they’re expecting you.
model.why: Sensible interim advice; prepares for possible intervention

model.text: Very important safety-net: if you collapse, the pain becomes severe, or you bleed heavily, call 999 and say you may have an ectopic pregnancy — don’t wait. Can you tell me back what you’re going to do now?
model.why: Explicit emergency safety-net and checks understanding

model.text: Call my husband, head to the Early Pregnancy Unit, and 999 if I collapse or it gets much worse.
Exactly right. I’m sorry you’re going through this — you’ve done everything correctly, and they’ll look after you. I’ll make that call now.

Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

playbook.diagnosis: Do not falsely reassure: “Because your period is late and you have this pain with spotting and feeling faint, I have to take seriously a pregnancy settling outside the womb — an ectopic — and that needs checking today.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Sometimes a pregnancy settles in the wrong place — in the tube instead of the womb. We can’t tell over the phone, and because it can become dangerous, the safe thing is a scan and a blood test today, not tomorrow.”

management.reflectIce: “I can hear how frightened you are that you might be losing a baby — whatever this turns out to be, ringing now was absolutely the right thing, and I’m going to make sure you’re seen quickly.”
management.psychosocial: Help her mobilise support (call partner), arrange transport, and give clear interim advice (nil-by-mouth, simple analgesia) so she feels held, not abandoned, while she gets there.

pitfalls.intro: Candidates do not fail this station on gynaecology knowledge — they fail on slow prioritisation, false reassurance, and forgetting that a telephone consultation has its own craft.

items.fail: A full SOCRATES, bowel and urinary screen before asking the one question that changes everything — “when was your last period, and could you be pregnant?”
items.why: “Fails to prioritise data gathering.” In any woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain, pregnancy status is the pivot; reaching it at minute eight reads as unsafe.
items.fix: LMP, contraception and the possibility of pregnancy inside the first three minutes, signposted: “Some quick but really important questions first…”

items.fail: Arranging a pregnancy test and a review “once we have the result” — running it like a routine query.
items.why: “Does not recognise urgency / unsafe management plan.” A 6-week LMP with unilateral pain and dizziness is a same-day EPAU presentation; the test must never delay the referral.
items.fix: Refer same-day while the test happens in parallel: “I’m arranging for you to be seen today either way — the test fine-tunes what they do, it doesn’t decide whether you go.”

items.fail: Never opening the record — missing the treated chlamydia and the ovarian-cyst surgery sitting in the notes.
items.why: “Did not use information already available.” The SCA penalises ignoring the record as much as re-asking it — and both items raise ectopic risk.
items.fix: Use the stem aloud: “I can see you had chlamydia treated years ago and an operation near the tubes — that makes me extra careful today.”

items.fail: Hearing “we’ve been trying for a baby” and responding with a protocol line, then continuing the checklist.
items.why: “Does not respond to cues at the moment they are offered.” Hope and dread arriving together is the emotional substance of this station.
items.fix: Name both sides before moving on: “So this pain has come at a moment of real hope — I can hear how frightening that makes it.” Then act decisively.

items.fail: False reassurance to soften a phone call — “I’m sure it’s nothing, probably a little cyst.”
items.why: Examiners punish false reassurance harder than bluntness: “did not share concerns honestly”. If this is an ectopic, “it’s nothing” is dangerous.
items.fix: Honest and contained: “It may well turn out fine — but the one thing I must rule out today is a pregnancy in the wrong place, because that can become serious quickly.”

items.fail: No telephone craft — never establishing where she is, who is with her, or how she will get to the unit; no call-back number agreed.
items.why: The SCA marks skills appropriate to the modality. Remote stations fail on “did not establish the practical context or a safe transfer”.
items.fix: Location, company, transport: agree exactly where she is going, who is taking her, that the unit expects her — and what she does if anything changes en route.

items.fail: Safety-netting with “call us back if it gets worse”.
items.why: “Safety-netting non-specific.” For suspected ectopic the net is 999-level and must be spelt out.
items.fix: “If you collapse, the pain suddenly worsens, your shoulder tip starts hurting or the bleeding gets heavy — that is 999, not the surgery.” Then check back what she will do now.

timeMap.d: Let her tell the story. On the phone your ears are your examination — note breathlessness, pauses, pain in her voice.
Pain, LMP (6 weeks!), contraception stopped, trying to conceive, bleeding/spotting, shoulder-tip pain, dizziness on standing. The ectopic question must be asked by minute 4.
"Late period, trying for a baby, one-sided pain, shoulder ache, lightheaded — I have to treat this as a possible ectopic pregnancy until proven otherwise."
Same-day EPAU / A&E — today, not tomorrow. Pregnancy test before leaving but do NOT wait on it. Confirm transport and who is with her.
999 triggers: collapse, sudden severe pain, heavy bleeding. Acknowledge what this might mean for a wanted pregnancy. Confirm she can repeat the plan back.

wordPics.fail: Anchors on appendicitis or UTI; never asks LMP or contraception; books a routine face-to-face for tomorrow; safety-nets with "ring back if worse"; the emotional line — "we've been trying" — goes completely unanswered.
wordPics.pass: Asks LMP and recognises possible ectopic; elicits at least one red flag; sends her to EPAU/A&E the same day; gives 999 triggers; acknowledges the pregnancy hope at least briefly.
wordPics.exc: Names the ectopic possibility honestly but without panic; checks shoulder-tip pain, orthostatic symptoms AND bleeding unprompted; arranges transfer while explicitly not delaying for the urine test; confirms transport and company; holds the emotional weight ("whatever this turns out to be, ringing now was right").

avoid.dont: "It's probably nothing serious, but let's get you checked just in case."
avoid.instead: "One thing we always have to rule out with this picture is a pregnancy outside the womb — that's why you need to be seen today."
avoid.why: Minimising language buries the urgency; honest naming earns the management mark.

avoid.dont: "Can you come in tomorrow morning and we'll examine you?"
avoid.instead: "This can't wait for the surgery. I want you in the early pregnancy unit this afternoon — let's sort out how you get there."
avoid.why: A routine review of a possible ectopic is the single fastest way to fail this station.

avoid.instead: "I can hear how much this pregnancy would mean. You did the right thing ringing now."
avoid.why: "Don't worry" dismisses; naming the hope relates.

items.fail: Arranging a pregnancy test and a review “once we have the result” — running it like a routine query.
items.why: “Does not recognise urgency / unsafe management plan.” A 6-week LMP with unilateral pain and dizziness is a same-day EPAU presentation; the test must never delay the referral.
items.fix: Refer same-day while the test happens in parallel: “I’m arranging for you to be seen today either way — the test fine-tunes what they do, it doesn’t decide whether you go.”

items.fail: Never opening the record — missing the treated chlamydia and the ovarian-cyst surgery sitting in the notes.
items.why: “Did not use information already available.” The SCA penalises ignoring the record as much as re-asking it — and both items raise ectopic risk.
items.fix: Use the stem aloud: “I can see you had chlamydia treated years ago and an operation near the tubes — that makes me extra careful today.”

items.fail: Hearing “we’ve been trying for a baby” and responding with a protocol line, then continuing the checklist.
items.why: “Does not respond to cues at the moment they are offered.” Hope and dread arriving together is the emotional substance of this station.
items.fix: Name both sides before moving on: “So this pain has come at a moment of real hope — I can hear how frightening that makes it.” Then act decisively.

items.fail: False reassurance to soften a phone call — “I’m sure it’s nothing, probably a little cyst.”
items.why: Examiners punish false reassurance harder than bluntness: “did not share concerns honestly”. If this is an ectopic, “it’s nothing” is dangerous.
items.fix: Honest and contained: “It may well turn out fine — but the one thing I must rule out today is a pregnancy in the wrong place, because that can become serious quickly.”

items.fail: No telephone craft — never establishing where she is, who is with her, or how she will get to the unit; no call-back number agreed.
items.why: The SCA marks skills appropriate to the modality. Remote stations fail on “did not establish the practical context or a safe transfer”.
items.fix: Location, company, transport: agree exactly where she is going, who is taking her, that the unit expects her — and what she does if anything changes en route.

items.fail: Safety-netting with “call us back if it gets worse”.
items.why: “Safety-netting non-specific.” For suspected ectopic the net is 999-level and must be spelt out.
items.fix: “If you collapse, the pain suddenly worsens, your shoulder tip starts hurting or the bleeding gets heavy — that is 999, not the surgery.” Then check back what she will do now.
